query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature and irradiation-exposed applications, what intervention could improve mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding specific refractory elements to refractory high-entropy alloys can improve their mechanical performance while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast or wrought refractory high-entropy alloys with potential defects and varying elemental distributions
generation.intervention: Composition change through the addition of specific refractory elements such as W, Ta, Cr, V, Mo, Nb, or Hf
generation.structural_mediator: Grain refinement and solid solution strengthening
generation.mechanism: The added refractory elements enhance high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance by stabilizing the solid solution, reducing defect formation, and promoting grain refinement
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved mechanical performance, including increased yield strength and ductility, at high temperatures and under irradiation, while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability
generation.baseline: Conventional refractory high-entropy alloys without the addition of specific refractory elements
generation.boundary: The improvement in mechanical performance is expected to be significant at high temperatures (above 800°C) and under irradiation conditions, but may be limited at room temperature due to potential brittleness
generation.uncertainty: The optimal combination and concentration of refractory elements to achieve the desired improvement in mechanical performance while maintaining stability are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare refractory high-entropy alloy samples with and without the addition of specific refractory elements, and subject them to high-temperature and irradiation exposure conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of refractory elements does not result in a significant improvement in mechanical performance at high temperatures and under irradiation, while maintaining thermal and irradiation stability, the hypothesis is falsified

Combining the two approaches above, the authors have recently developed a refractory low-activation HEA based on W-Ta-Cr-V. Its response to loop formation under ion irradiation and He implantation is enhanced compared to previously developed W-based alloys, showing no noticeable dislocation loop formation and smaller He bubbles with no radiation-induced segregation at grain boundaries upon heavy ion irradiation and He implantation, respectively. However, this quaternary RHEA demonstrated Cr- and V-rich precipitates which could be detrimental to mechanical properties in terms of embrittlement. In this study, a design strategy to further improve the overall response of the W-Ta-Cr-V RHEA is introduced and resulted in the development of a quinary RHEA with improved resistance to high-temperature and irradiation environments. In the process of pursuing high-performance materials, the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [] were introduced. The preeminent properties (such as high strength [,], good corrosion resistance [,,], fine tribological properties [,], remarkable softening resistance [,], and outstanding irradiation tolerance [,,,], etc.) enhance the application competitiveness of HEAs under extreme environments. Among them, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [], which are characterized by a high melting point and prepared by methods such as vacuum arc melting, suspension melting, spark plasma sintering [], and wire electric discharge machining [], are expected to play a role in future high-temperature applications []. Compared with conventional alloys, HEAs, especially the body-centered cubic (BCC) structured ones composed of refractory elements, exhibit better irradiation tolerance for the extreme lattice distortions and chemical complexity, such as prominent resistance to hardening [,], suppressed dislocation evolution [,,], low volume swelling rate [,], and reduced radiation-induced segregation [,,], etc. Hence, the HEAs are considered to be a promising candidate for nuclear structural materials [,]

In recent years, a set of alloys based on several principal elements has been developed (). The configurational entropy of mixing in multicomponent alloys tends to stabilize the solid solution based on simple underlying face-centered cubic (FCC) or body-centered cubic (BCC) crystal structures. Equiatomic compositions maximize this entropic term, promoting random solutions versus intermetallic phases or phase decomposition. Some of the high-entropy alloys (HEAs) show superior mechanical response to traditional materials, which generally links to dislocation properties. These materials can display high hardness values, high yield strengths, large ductility, excellent fatigue resistance, and good fracture toughness. W-based refractory HEAs have been recently developed in the context of high-temperature applications, showing high melting temperature (above 2873 K) and superior mechanical properties at high temperatures compared to Ni-based superalloys and nanocrystalline W () samples (, ). The equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy was chosen to analyze the effect of each constituent elemental by the subtraction method and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were studied. Among these alloys, HfMoNbTaTi has the best mechanical performance, that is, 27% compressive strain at room temperature and yield strength 367 MPa at 1400 °C. HfMoNbTaTi has great potential for elevated-temperature applications. As the alloy system does not contain very expensive elements such as Re and Ru, it is cost competitive for high-temperature applications like Nb-Hf-Ti alloys in space vehicles. Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are still required for high-temperature applications in the air. According to the experiment results, the effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on mechanical properties of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr alloys were described. For higher room-temperature strength, one should add an element which interacts frequently with the alloy, such as Mo.
